articles.title: Bigg Boss 20: Qazi Touqeer breaks down emotionally after Salman Khan bashes ScoutOP and Yung DSA for their behaviour; netizens slam the makers
articles.summary: The latest episode of Bigg Boss 20 witnessed an emotional moment when Qazi Touqeer broke down while trying to speak to Salman Khan.
articles.body: The latest episode of Bigg Boss 20 witnessed an emotional moment when Qazi Touqeer broke down while trying to speak to Salman Khan. During the episode, Salman addressed the issue involving Qazi, ScoutOP, Mahhi Vij and Love Gill, questioning Scout’s behaviour and the way he handled the situation.As Qazi became emotional, he asked, “Can I talk, sir?” His reaction came amid the discussion surrounding the treatment of contestants and the incident involving food being given to him.During the conversation, Mahhi Vij expressed her displeasure over the food arrangements, saying, “Inka bas chale ye log khana le le haath se, itne gande se khana dete hai ye log” (If it were up to them, they would snatch the food from people’s hands. They serve food in such a disgusting manner). Her comment added to the discussion about the conditions inside the house.Qazi added, “The doctors asked me if I had pain in my joints, but I said no because I wanted to entertain. I’m good now, but I wasn’t well back then.” (Doctors ne mujhse poocha tha ki kya mere joints mein dard hai, lekin maine mana kar diya kyunki main entertain karna chahta tha. Ab main theek hoon, lekin us waqt meri tabiyat theek nahi thi.)Salman then confronted Scout about the incident, questioning his actions and his intentions behind allowing Love to give food to Qazi. He suggested that Scout’s actions could have been an attempt to create a favourable impression on television. Salman said, “Aapko jab Qazi se problem thi toh aap kyun gaye, why did you let Love go and give him food, number banane the ki dekho main bimar aadmi ko khana de raha hun, TV pe bohot acha lagega” (If you had a problem with Qazi, why did you go? Why did you let Love go and give him food? Did you want to score brownie points by showing that you were feeding a sick person, thinking it would look very good on television?).Reacting to Salman’s remarks, ScoutOP clarified that he had no such intention. He said, “Jaisa maine bola, mera koi intention nahi tha, genuinely” (As I said, I genuinely had no such intention). However, Salman remained unconvinced by his explanation and continued to criticise his approach.Salman went on to reprimand Scout for his behaviour, calling his approach “wahiyat” and “heartless”. He further pointed out that even people in jail are provided with food and water, questioning the manner in which the situation had been handled. He said, “Aapka tarika bada hi wahiyat, bada hi heartless hai. Jail mein bhi issue achhe se khana dete hai, mug se pani dete hai” (Your way of handling things is absolutely disgusting and heartless. Even in jail, people are given proper food and water in a mug).However, netizens had mixed reactions with many calling out the makers for their alleged bias toward Qazi.One user wrote, “Scout OP openly saying makers log agenda chala rahe hai. Openly bola ye log apan ko apas me bhidana chah rahe hai. Bhai bande me guts hai. He openly told Qazi ki tumhari 100 baatein nahi boli. Qazi ke paas 1 bhi jawab nahi tha.” Another user mentioned, “Yeh Kya Hai Bhai As per Maker's Only Qazi and Mahi giving content and as per Audience only #AamrapaliDubey #LoveGill #YungDsa #ScoutOp #Arishfa giving cotent.”One more user was like, “The way #ScoutOP stood up for himself, fearlessly put forward his perspective, and refused to bow down under pressure is truly commendable. His courage to speak his mind.” “When pressure hits, most people fold. ScoutOP didn’t. He stood his ground and put his point across clearly. That kind of backbone is rare,” wrote a fan.Get the latest TV News, TV Shows and more. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: The new Apple TV could have a built-in mic and a remote with a speaker
articles.summary: The overdue Apple TV refresh makes it easier to talk to Siri and find your remote.
articles.body: The latest rumors are that the new Apple TV will have a built-in microphone, while the upgraded remote will get a speaker. The mic would let users control the set-top box using Siri without having to speak into the remote or a connected HomePod device. That could also let the Apple TV serve as a simple smart home hub — controlling thermostats and locking doors — without the need to hunt for the remote. If you happen to misplace the remote, the new integrated speaker should make it easier to track down. It could play an audio alert to guide you to its location, whether it got carelessly kicked under the couch or a child mischievously hid it in a drawer. This is on top of the upgrade to an A19 chip that will power Siri AI. The Apple TV is expected to start shipping on October 30th, alongside the refreshed HomePod Mini.

Over the past couple of years, we’ve seen multiple reports that Apple was working on a new smart home product , but now it seems the product has a name and a launch date. The HomeView will reportedly be available in two models — one designed for countertops and the other to be mounted on walls.

This would be Apple’s most serious bet on the smart home to date, after it failed to get much traction for its HomeKit software framework or its HomePod smart speaker.

Gurman reports that on Tuesday, Apple will also be unveiling updated versions of two other home devices, namely the Apple TV set-top box and the HomePod mini. Earlier this week, he said that Apple plans to announce a partnership with LG to create a smart lock, a thermostat, and a doorbell.

articles.title: Ramayan’s Arun Govil and Dipika Chikhlia reunite after 39 years for an upcoming project, a social drama about a 150-year-old shop
articles.summary: For generations of viewers, Arun Govil and Dipika Chikhlia remain synonymous with Lord Ram and Goddess Sita from Ramanand Sagar’s iconic television series
articles.body: For generations of viewers, Arun Govil and Dipika Chikhlia remain synonymous with Lord Ram and Goddess Sita from Ramanand Sagar’s iconic television series Ramayan. Nearly four decades after the show first aired in 1987, the much-loved on-screen pair is reuniting for a film that explores a very different story.Titled Notice, the upcoming social drama is directed by Pradeep Gupta and will premiere on the streaming platform Waves on November 6.The film revolves around a 150-year-old shop that faces the threat of demolition due to development. Arun Govil plays a man who takes on a corrupt system to protect the shop and fight for justice, while Dipika Chikhlia portrays his wife, who stands firmly by him throughout his struggle.Speaking to Mid-Day, producer-actor Aditya Pratap Singh Raghuvanshi explained why he believes the Ramayan duo is the right fit for the film. He said the story would resonate with people who have lost their homes or businesses because of development projects.“The story has a 150-year-old shop at its centre. All those who have lost their homes or shops due to development will identify with it. And who can tell this story better than Ram and Sita? Where there is a fight between truth and untruth, Ram and Sita’s jodi has to be there. You can call it a modern-day Ramayan,” Raghuvanshi told Mid-Day.The makers have opted for an OTT release to take the film to a wider audience. Raghuvanshi also told the publication that Waves’ subscriber base could help Notice reach viewers across the country.He pointed out that while cinema audiences today largely have an urban outlook, Govil and Chikhlia continue to enjoy a strong connection with television audiences. articles.title: What a child’s iPhone looks like with iOS 27’s new parental controls
articles.summary: Apple has offered parental controls on the iPhone for years, and for most of that time they worked in reverse.
articles.body: Apple has offered parental controls on the iPhone for years, and for most of that time they worked in reverse. A child got a fully stocked phone, and a parent spent the following weekend inside Screen Time menus, switching off whatever didn't belong. The tools did their job, but only after the phone had already changed hands.iOS 27, which brought Apple's reworked parental controls to iPhone, iPad and Mac last month, moves most of that work to the very start. What a child unlocks is a phone that asks before it does almost anything new, whether that's installing an app, opening a website or adding a contact. The more useful thing to understand, for any parent setting one up, is where that asking stops.A child's iPhone now begins with only the apps a parent choseSetup starts with a Child Account, which Apple requires for anyone under 13 and allows up to 18. The account does a fair amount on its own. Adult websites are limited, films and music are held to age ratings, and the App Store applies age-based restrictions before a parent has touched a single toggle.The visible change comes a few screens later, where a parent now decides which apps exist on the phone at all. Apple offers three routes: a bare set of essentials such as Phone, Find My and Mail, a starter set it recommends for the child's age, or a list built one app at a time. Even Apple's own built-in apps are up for selection, so a seven-year-old's iPhone no longer has to carry the Stocks app simply because every iPhone does.The home screen a child sees on day one can hold half a dozen icons.Everything after that arrives by request. Ask to Buy, an older feature that carries straight into iOS 27, sends every App Store download, free or paid, and every in-app purchase to a parent for approval. Put that alongside the new setup, and there isn't an app on the phone a parent hasn't signed off on.That also puts a lot of weight on what a parent approves. Saying yes to WhatsApp or Instagram means saying yes to an entire world of people and content that Apple's own approval system doesn't reach, which is where the rest of this update comes in.The asking is tightest inside Apple's own appsAsk to Browse brings the Ask to Buy logic to Safari. Tap a link to a site the child hasn't visited before, and a request screen appears in place of the page, while the parent gets a message with the link so they can look the site over first. It is on by default for under-13s, and works the same way on a child's iPad and Mac. For teenagers, it stays off unless a parent switches it on, which seems like the sensible default. A 15-year-old researching a school project would otherwise send a request every few minutes, and a parent stuck in a meeting would be the one fielding them.Contacts follow the same pattern across Messages, FaceTime and the Phone app. A child who wants to add a new tuition teacher or a friend from the school bus sends a request, and a parent approves it with a tap. Contact approvals existed last year too, but iOS 27 folds them into setup, so the list is agreed on before the first call goes out.Then there is the part where a parent's yes or no doesn't come into it. Communication Safety, on by default for anyone under 18, already blurs nudity in Messages and FaceTime and asks the child whether they still want to see it. With iOS 27, violent and gory photos and videos are blocked outright, whether the child is sending or receiving them, including during live FaceTime calls. Apple has made that call on the parent's behalf.All of this is strongest inside Apple's own apps, though. Ask to Browse covers Safari, and contact approvals cover Messages, FaceTime and Phone. In India, where a child's social life is far more likely to run on WhatsApp than iMessage, that boundary matters. Apple does give developers the tools to plug into the same system, from blurring sensitive images and routing new in-app contacts to a parent, to tailoring an app to a child's age range without ever seeing their birthday, but each app has to adopt them. Until the apps a child spends most time in do that, the approval that matters is the one made at the App Store.Apple now has a view on how much screen time is enoughTime Allowances, which replace App Limits, split a child's apps into Games, Entertainment and Social Media, with a daily ceiling for each. What's new is that Apple suggests the numbers. Based on the child's age and expert research, a parent sees a recommended allowance for every category, which they can keep, raise or cut. The guidance draws on health experts including the American Academy of Pediatrics, whose Family Media Plan Apple is adapting into a guide for families.It is a small change built on a fair assumption, that most parents would rather start from a number than a blank field. The categories are Apple's too, so where an app lands decides which allowance it eats into, and a video app used for maths revision counts the same as one used for cat clips. Schedules work alongside all this, greying out restricted apps during school hours or any other window a parent sets.The parent's side is built for decisions that can't waitThe parent's side has been rebuilt for decisions made in the moment. Tap a child's name under Family in Settings, and Screen Time now opens on average daily use and the most-used apps, with three buttons up top to pause the device, allow unlimited use or change the schedule, none of which touch the allowances underneath. They're meant for dinner, a long drive, or a child pleading for ten more minutes to finish a level, which is when most screen-time decisions get made anyway. Screen Time Passcode Notifications, meanwhile, alert a parent if their passcode is entered on the child's device, a quiet admission that children are rather good at watching fingers.There is one condition attached. Every device in the Family Sharing group, a parent's Apple Watch included, needs to be on the latest software for the new Screen Time to work, and Apple says some features won't be available in every region or language.What a child unwraps on iOS 27, then, is a smaller phone than the one their parents carry, and one that asks before it grows. The work that used to happen in Settings after the handover now happens before it. What's left for a parent is the one decision Apple can't make for them, which apps get approved in the first place, because past that point, how much asking happens depends on the app.You use AI every day. articles.title: Inside the mini factory where GM builds its EV future
articles.summary: GM’s new battery cell development mini factory is essential to the company’s effort to slash EV costs. But can it develop its batteries in enough time to compete with China?
articles.body: If you’re driving through GM’s sprawling campus in Warren, Michigan, you’d likely ignore the pair of adjacent, anonymous white buildings tucked away in the upper reaches of the 710-acre space. Inside those buildings, which total half a million square feet together, is a massive construction project that’s still in progress. Once completed, it will house GM’s new Battery Cell Development Center, where the automaker is working furiously to build new prototype cells with the goal of slashing the cost of its EVs. GM has to build faster and cheaper to meet its goal of selling affordable EVs in much higher volumes. Those EVs will have to compete not only with longtime sales leader Tesla, but also with the flood of Chinese EVs that, sooner or later, will land in the US. And while EV sales in the US appear to be leveling out, America has a long way to go before it can credibly compete with China, the world’s leading EV market. The number of shoppers interested in new and used EVs spiked when gas prices rose 40 percent this year as a result of the war in Iran — but mostly in models priced lower than the average $50,000 cost of a new vehicle today. While GM sells more EVs in the US than any other company after Tesla, most of its lineup is still too expensive thanks to a battery pack that makes up 30 to 40 percent of the total cost. During an early September tour, after putting on a hard hat, safety glasses, and a hi-vis vest, I saw up close the tools GM will use to build these newer, cheaper batteries: huge vats for mixing cell slurry, coating machines that deposit electrode material onto film, and machines for a dozen other steps in the process of turning minerals into cells that hold and deliver energy. The plant I toured will be a low-volume factory that lets engineers prototype the higher-volume production to come from giant, billion-dollar factories. The new facility suggests GM is playing a long game, working to develop new cells that use less — or none — of the minerals China controls globally. Although US scientists developed the original R&D on most new cell chemistries, Asian companies were the ones to develop, refine, and put those chemistries into volume production. The 15-year Chinese effort that gave the country global control of supply and processing for minerals used in today’s cells, especially cobalt, nickel, and rare earths, means future cells must use different minerals to escape the country’s dominance. One example: GM’s new LMR, or lithium manganese-rich, cells use very little cobalt or nickel. A second: This spring GM announced it’s working with startup Peak Energy on sodium-ion cells for energy storage. Getting such new chemistries out of the lab and into volume production can last a decade or more. But GM doesn’t have that long. China may already be selling its EVs to Americans by then. The company’s battery engineers are confident that using the new facility inside those anonymous buildings 15 miles north of Detroit can launch new cell chemistries and formats for EVs and battery energy-storage systems in less time than predicted. The company’s future will rest on whether it can succeed. [Image: An engineer inspects a roll press system at GM’s new Battery Cell Development Center. In June, GM battery czar Kurt Kelty told me the new Battery Cell Development Center, or BCDC, will provide “the critical bridge from R&D lab to production” by combining virtual modeling, physical test capabilities, and small-scale production lines. The aim is to fill the missing link between creating and prototyping new cells and getting them into high-volume production. BCDC head Mo Gallegos puts the total cost at $900 million. At maximum production, the BCDC might produce 4 to 5 gigawatt-hours of cells. But the goal isn’t quantity; it’s quality. Inside the 500,000-square-foot lab, I saw much of the machinery needed to fabricate a cell, from mixing slurry for the coating that forms a cell electrode to the charging hardware that energizes a finished cell for the first time. The mini factory will be used for multiple cell chemistries and different formats, starting with prismatic cells. Its purpose is to test industrial cell manufacturing processes, proving and optimizing production techniques and recipes before they’re implemented at scale. While the BCDC will produce actual working cells, it will do so in far lower volumes and at slower speeds than the production lines at full-scale cell plants. GM’s battery developers will then transfer the knowledge gained from this process testing to its cell production partners that will take the new designs to full-scale volume. Those would likely include the two plants operated by Ultium Cells LLC, the joint cell production venture between GM and its cell partner, LG Energy Solution. The first plant in Warren, Ohio, opened in 2022 and makes large-format nickel-manganese-cobalt-aluminium pouch cells for GM’s line of EVs (excluding the 2027 Bolt). The second, in Spring Hills, Tennessee, opened in early 2024 and now produces lithium-ion phosphate cells for battery energy storage. Of the two BCDC buildings, the first houses anode and cathode fabrication on opposite sides, with electrode assembly in the middle. A bridge transports rolls of electrode film to the second building, where the cells are assembled, charged, and tested for eight to 11 days. The second stories house supplies of the metals, films, and components needed, as well as a very substantial set of HVAC equipment to keep the processes sterile, dust-free, and at the right temperature. The BCDC is slated to produce its first test cells — LMR prismatic cells — in the fourth quarter of this year. But they won’t go into volume production at the Ultium plant in Spring Hill until 2028. Once tests for LMR cells get underway, it will add the sodium-ion prismatic cells it’s developing for BESS with startup Peak Energy. [Image: A close-up view of foil battery material before it is incorporated into the cell assembly process. The problem the BCDC is meant to solve is the chasm between creating new cell chemistries at a small scale and cranking them out in massive quantities in the hundreds of thousands or millions. Taking them all the way through development to commercialization means understanding how to build them; that requires testing production processes and methods to ensure the quality of the finished cells as well as their quantity. You can think of getting a cell to market in four phases: creating a new chemistry, testing early prototypes, figuring out how to build it, and then ramping up volume production. The first phase has been centered in GM’s Kettering R&D laboratory for decades. It created and tested new chemistries and cells for the pioneering EV1, the 2011 Chevrolet Volt, and the LMR chemistry the company plans to launch in 2028. But it’s limited to proving out a chemistry one cell at a time, in “coin” or small pouch formats. GM brought the second phase in-house when it opened its Wallace Battery Cell Innovation Center in 2023. That lab takes new chemistries and expands them into large-format cells up to 200 amp-hours. Wallace can fabricate these new cells in tiny batches of a few dozen, testing whether a new chemistry will continue to perform and remain practical in cells identical to those to be used in end products. Now, the third phase has arrived in the BCDC, right next door to Wallace. It will use real-world cell fabrication and battery assembly machinery to build thousands of cells a day — ideally assuring the ultimate ramp-up in a bigger plant goes smoothly. And it’s been built with double the floor space used initially to allow for future expansion, multiple chemistries, and multiple cell formats. Historically, those second and third phases were done by battery manufacturers. They were the missing link between a new chemistry and volume production — virtually always done overseas. Wallace and the BCDC together give GM almost 1 million square feet of battery development space. (GM declined to specify how many employees worked at either facility, saying it varied.) The fourth and last phase is commercial production at scale, whether at Ultium Cells or other high-volume plants. To compare the scale of each phase, Kettering R&D might produce 1 liter of slurry with which to coat electrode film to test individual cells. The Wallace lab takes that to 40 liters at a time. Now, BCDC will be able to make 1,500 to 2,000 liters at a time in a single process — whereas high-volume cell plants will run several dozen identical copies of that process at once, or two orders of magnitude more. [Image: A GM engineer inspects equipment that gives battery developers a hands-on way to study and refine material handling before full-scale cell production. Before any physical fabrication starts, cell engineers use virtualization throughout the process. Agility in developing and refining new designs fast comes from using “digital twins” to simulate processes well before production hardware enters the process, said Radu Theyyunni, GM’s director of virtual engineering for global propulsion. In the automotive world, a well-known example is the use of CAD software to model structural designs and crash responses. Over decades, simulations let carmakers speed up their engineering and substantially cut the number of costly prototype vehicles they must inevitably crash to confirm their safety. Similarly, from the internal behavior of new cell chemistries to the steps of manufacturing each component — how thoroughly molecules are blended in a “high-shear double planetary mixer” to produce slurry, for instance — the time saved through modeling can cut weeks and months out of the timetable to get a new cell from the lab to market. More recently, GM has leaned heavily on AI in a variety of different virtualization models. Informed by its huge trove of 10 years of prior battery data, Theyyunni said its large language models now predict the results of dozens of minor chemistry changes and process variations far faster than any physical prototyping and testing could. Those results have proven extremely accurate, he said, when they are transferred into real-world prototyping. At the chemistry level, this simulation lets GM model “what happens if we add more silicon, what happens if you lower the cobalt content,” said Theyyunni. “We can simulate what that would be in a couple of days,” added Kelty. That lets the company tweak production processes as needed, then model again. If done by a cell maker overseas, that process could take months. Intensive modeling of the molecule blending in slurry mixers let GM cut mixing time by half against the recommended industry practice, Theyyunni said, with no impact on quality or cell performance. Overall, Theyyunni said, the company expects to take a cell through the end-to-end process in “roughly half the time” — although GM declined to quantify timelines or put a number on the time saved. Previously, Kelty suggested it could let GM shave up to a year off development of promising new cell chemistries. The modeling spans every level of vehicle development: a digital twin of the entire EV; one for the battery pack; one for the cells inside; a digital twin of the electrode that models particle behavior on the electrodes as the cell discharges and recharges; and finally a twin at the atomic level to model lithium diffusion through the electrodes and electrolyte. The methods transfer easily and simply among chemistries. For battery cells, “atomistic modeling is chemistry agnostic,” Kelty said. To go from NMCA to sodium-ion cells, “we just change the atoms in the model.” After all, “the core equations for quantum mechanics are well known,” added Theyyunni. [Image: Mo Gallegos, head of GM’s new Battery Cell Development Center, with machinery that lets its engineers prototype production of new cells before transferring the process to full-scale factories. Simulating cell behavior on an atom-by-atom level, even before simulating the entire production process to build the cell in volume, takes a huge amount of computing power. During our tour, Gallegos noted the battery development complex draws more power than any other single part of the sprawling Warren campus. But the company has long done intensive computing, starting well before the modern era of EVs. Soon after the first emission regulations came into force half a century ago, GM began to use computers to model the phases of gasoline combustion inside its engines. Over time, as engines acquired multiple valves, multiple cams, variable valve timing, direct injection, turbochargers, and the growing array of hardware to make an inherently wasteful combustion process more efficient, they came to rely on constantly more powerful computer models. A specific example might be modeling the formation of soot particles within diesel combustion — and how to reduce them. That experience and available compute power let the company “unlock a lot of value” because it was “comfortable applying these multi-physics, highly detailed tools across lots of different domains where they’ve probably never been applied before,” said Theyyunni. During the tour, Theyyunni said the company’s compute power is second within the US only to the country’s national laboratories. And “the pace of growth in atomistic modeling is fast,” Theyyunni added, suggesting that over the past six months the company’s AI capabilities have expanded significantly. The combustion engine side of the house is now aggressively adding AI to its tool chest, though the cell modelers seem to feel they’re still ahead of the curve. The atomic and process modeling done within developing LMR cells, said Theyyunni, required three times the compute capacity that modeling the combustion processes for a gasoline engine does. Kelty is clearly energized by the possibilities of these new AI-informed modeling and simulation tools. Over the long haul, he said, “We want to get rid of testing” — or at least greatly reduce physical testing of prototype cells and their production methods. Less physical testing to develop and refine new cells would give GM more agility to respond to real-world test data. The ultimate goal, Kelty suggested, would be for the system to do its own R&D to the point that its AI models could “synthesize a new cell chemistry” on its own. But they’re not there yet, he said. Meanwhile, every large global battery maker has full-cycle development labs very similar to GM’s. Those let them figure out how to build cell chemistries that come in from R&D labs, automakers, consumer electronics companies, and many other sources. But few carmakers aside from Tesla have joint-venture cell plants to make cells they design, as GM does. And even fewer have the full set of R&D-to-prototype-to-process-to-production labs. Most of the world’s carmakers continue to rely on their cell partners to do parts of that process, in part because it costs a lot — both in compute power and physical plants. GM is betting its investment will give it an edge in speed and agility bringing new cells to market. We won’t know for years to come whether that bet will pay off.

articles.title: How Apple can win the smart home
articles.summary: New hardware could put Apple back in the race, but software will determine whether it wins.
articles.body: This week, Apple is hosting its first-ever dedicated smart home event. While the company hasn’t shared details about what it will reveal at the “Welcome Home experience” in New York City on Tuesday, October 13th, it doesn’t take an army of internet sleuths to deduce we’ll get news about Apple Home — specifically, new hardware. Apple finally seems to be taking the smart home seriously. According to Bloomberg, Apple will release a smart home display alongside a refreshed HomePod Mini and Apple TV. The display, which MacRumors reports may be called HomeView, is arguably Apple’s first dedicated Apple Home hardware since it launched the HomeKit platform in 2014. As exciting as this is (and I’ll be there in person to check it out), the real shift will be bringing Siri AI and Apple Intelligence into the home. Apple is years behind Google and Amazon in smart-home hardware, but success in the home depends far more on software. That’s where Apple could leapfrog the competition. New home hardware is long overdue. Apple announced the HomePod Mini on October 13th, 2020, six years to the day from this week’s event, and the newest Apple TV 4K is now four years old. And those aren’t dedicated smart home devices; they’re more content-consumption gadgets with a side of home automation. The new smart display is reportedly designed to be the heart of Apple Home, marking a complete reboot of the ecosystem, and Apple Home users have wanted it for years. [Image: Smart displays, like this Echo Show 8, can be used to view footage from home security cameras. The smart display category has a bumpy history. Amazon and Google have launched several generations of these voice- and touchscreen-controlled smart speakers that can control smart home gadgets like lights and locks, pull up doorbell camera feeds, and make video calls. But the category has seen very little innovation, and its best use case has been serving as a digital photo frame. Based on leaks, Apple’s product doesn’t sound that different from what’s come before. According to Bloomberg, it will have a 6-inch square display on a speaker base or as a wall-mounted option, facial recognition to show your personal messages and calendar, a minimalist touchscreen interface to control locks and thermostats, and FaceTime and intercom calls. Nothing groundbreaking, except the rumored price — $350, ouch. The difference has to be in the software and the smart assistant that powers it. Bloomberg reports the smart display will launch with a brand-new homeOS built around Siri AI. Generative AI has breathed new life into the smart home voice assistant by both making it easier to talk to and expanding its capabilities. Until now, Apple’s new Siri AI has been MIA from its HomePods and Apple TV; when you talk to those, the old Siri responds in its basic, functional way. [Image: Apple’s smart speakers: the HomePod and HomePod Mini. Rumors indicate that only the Mini will get a refresh this week to support Siri AI. Apple is the last of the big three to bring generative AI to its home assistant. Amazon and Google launched theirs last year, but Alexa Plus is only just starting to get it right, and Google’s Gemini for Home, an underpowered version of Gemini, is a confusing mess of capabilities. Now it’s Apple’s turn, and if the company can successfully merge its superpowered personal assistant on your iPhone with a superpowered assistant for your home, it may have a hit on its hands. That’s a very big if. So far, every company has hit significant roadblocks bringing a smarter assistant to the home. Apple announced Apple Intelligence in 2024, but Siri AI only arrived last month; a version of Alexa Plus was announced in 2023 but didn’t launch until 2025; Gemini for Home is still in an early access program and split into a weird hybrid model where its more capable version, Gemini Live, is restricted from interacting with the home. These cautious approaches are down to the fact that the home is a big, complicated, messy, multi-user environment that is hard to control. An agentic AI getting something wrong could have consequences far greater than accidentally sending an email. Smart home systems are connected to critical infrastructure like HVAC, locks, and security systems. Every home is different, with unique needs — there is no single plug-and-play solution. Progress has been made toward solving one of the smart home’s biggest challenges: interoperability, with open standards like Matter and Thread promising to make setting up and using a smart home easier. But these are protocols, not software. It’s the platforms that have to make the smart home work. Here is where Apple may have the edge. Four years ago, after helping found Matter, Apple rebuilt HomeKit’s underlying architecture and revamped the Home app, laying a strong foundation. That move also let Apple Home work with more devices from more manufacturers (previously, it was limited to those willing to go through the often arduous HomeKit approval process). [Image: The Apple Home app works across Apple devices. However, a smart home isn’t just about the devices you put in it. It’s about making them work together. That’s where Siri AI and Apple Intelligence could play a major role. While Apple used Gemini models to build Siri AI, Google itself has struggled to deliver a compelling experience in the home. So Apple’s opportunity lies in execution. Its more curated approach to third-party hardware has held it back, but it also means Apple arrives at this crucial moment with less technical debt and a cleaner foundation for building an AI-powered smart home. This will be the next level for the smart home; with reliable data and context, your home could know who’s in it, where they are, and what they need, and, combined with knowing the status of every device, become proactive. For example, it could alert you that the oven is on and no one is home, suggest turning off the AC when a window is left open, and route messages and notifications to the room you’re in. This is still a distant promise, however. Today, Apple Home has significant limitations: it doesn’t support every type of home device (no fridges, washing machines, or EV chargers); it can’t control every feature of many device types; and its automations are limited compared to the competition (notably lacking conditional programming options inside the app). All this makes the Home app very easy to use, but extremely underpowered. With Siri AI, Apple could unlock many of those capabilities via voice instead of building complicated menu interfaces. You could just tell Siri what you want your smart home to do. Alexa Plus offers this with the ability to create routines using your voice; Gemini for Home lets you use natural language in its Home app chatbot to set up automations; and many smart home companies are adopting AI in their apps to cut through UI complexity and make devices and features easier to use. A big question remains: do people really want a smart home? Many of us have spent years frustrated with systems that hold so much promise but routinely fail to deliver, leaving us spending weekends troubleshooting why the garage door won’t open. The truly dedicated have turned to Home Assistant, a powerful platform that can do almost anything you want, if you’re willing to do the work. But for most people, beyond a few solutions to specific problems, the smart home just isn’t worth it. To win in the smart home and bring the category mainstream, Apple needs more than just great hardware; it needs a superior software experience that makes the smart home easy to use. It needs to integrate seamlessly with third-party devices and deliver a consistent, reliable experience, relying on local control wherever possible and making sure products just work. Apple is reportedly partnering with LG and others to develop products for an “Apple Home Collection” that will add a layer of Apple polish to the smart home experience. While this might sound like going back to the walled garden of the HomeKit days, Matter ensures interoperability with other platforms. Apple can’t make everything for the smart home, but it can make sure that everything works with its platform. Most crucially, Apple will need to double down on its commitment to privacy and data security, especially as it opens the home to Apple Intelligence’s cloud-based capabilities. If Apple can deliver on all of this, its highly anticipated smart home display might justify its price. But the real test will be whether Siri can make the smart home live up to its promise.

articles.title: Former Plaud exec raises $26M for AI app that listens to you in the background | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Ambi is releasing apps for iPhone, Mac, and Apple Watch that enables ambient capture
articles.body:
One of the core promises of AI is that the more it knows about a person, the better it will be able to assist them with tasks and make appropriate suggestions, which, if you’ll believe the tech companies, requires apps and devices to listen, watch or record users’ activity all the time and gather all possible context.

There’s obviously privacy and data security concerns with anything that’s collecting data about you continuously. But startups are building such apps undeterred anyway, arming themselves with the belief that the market for personalized assistance is big enough to swallow such concerns.

Former Plaud exec Peter Mo is building Ambi to do something similar. The app aims to provide real-time intelligence and insights to people by listening to them all the time.

The company said on Monday that it has raised $26 million across multiple funding rounds led by Luminous Ventures, which has backed companies like Meituan and Unitree Robotics, and Original Design Manufacturer (ODM) Huaqin.

Ambi is also releasing apps for iPhones, Macs and Apple Watch. These apps act like meeting note-takers, but users can choose to have them listening so they can capture context all day.

Meeting note-taking companies have been working to automate tasks that follow once calls are done, based on the summaries and action items they gather during the conversation, and using multitudes of connectors to software systems. Ambi wants to take this a step further by having its agent start the work during the meeting itself.

The company’s promise is that its AI agent can proactively give you suggestions or surface relevant knowledge while you are in a meeting, based on your calendar, meetings, knowledge base, and web data. Users can also start a task on one device and continue it on another.

“The way we interact with intelligence is limited. Often the intelligence is trapped on the screen, and if you use hardware like Plaud, you need to wait for recording to transfer to the phone, upload to the cloud, and get intelligence after processing. That’s why we are building Ambi to use AI anytime and anywhere,” the company’s co-founder and CEO, Mo, told TechCrunch.

The company has ambitions to capture more information. Its upcoming desktop app will be able to look at the work that users do and store important parts in its memory to give more personalized suggestions. Apps like Littlebird or Minimi already do something similar.

The startup is also planning to launch its own hardware device, which will have a screen, a speaker, a camera, and microphones to capture context and display information.

Ambi’s launch comes amidst growing concerns around AI devices that don’t have enough indicators to suggest they are capturing data on people around the user. It is not clear if Ambi’s apps or its upcoming device will have enough indicators to alert third-parties that their conversations are being recorded if the user doesn’t disclose their use of Ambi’s tech.

Some meeting note-takers have even been sued because their tech recorded people’s conversation and data without their consent. Plus, the recent release of Apple’s Voice Intelligence feature, which transcribes speech continuously, has raised privacy concerns .

Mo said that users can turn off ambient data capture on Ambi’s apps and devices at any time, and the feature is off by default. The startup said it doesn’t store any recordings of users and encrypts the data, but it didn’t specify what kind of encryption it uses. Despite these measures, the onus of declaring ambient capture is still on the users. He classified this as an industry-wide problem.

“We have to inform our users that they have to tell others about ambient capture. We, as an industry, haven’t solved this problem [of disclosure]. We have tried to put the information about disclosure in every place possible, but if users try to hide the capture, we can’t just solve the problem,” he said.

Ambi currently has over 50 staff across offices in San Francisco, Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen. The company is hiring for its go-to-market function and AI engineers for working on speech recognition models.

articles.title: CMF’s first wireless speakers look like musical milk cartons
articles.summary: You can customize the appearance of the $59 CMF Speaker S and $109 CMF Speaker M by swapping colored knobs and panels or 3D printing your own.
articles.body: The CMF Speaker Series are the first portable Bluetooth speakers from the budget-focused brand that Nothing created but is in the process of spinning off into an India-based standalone subsidiary. As with many of CMF’s products, like the Headphone Pro that launched a year ago, the new speakers deliver affordability alongside unique designs and bright color options that help them stand out from the competition. While the company doesn’t directly cite a grocery store’s dairy aisle as the inspiration for its latest hardware, it’s hard not to look at these and immediately see electronic milk cartons. There are two versions of the CMF Speaker Series available starting today in white, dark gray, orange, and turquoise color options. The $59 CMF Speaker S is the smaller of the two and features a “custom-tuned” 45mm full-range driver paired with two passive radiators to help boost the presence of low-end frequencies. The larger $109 CMF Speaker M instead features two drivers including a 10W tweeter and a dedicated 25W woofer for improved bass performance and better separation of instruments and singers. [Image: The larger Speaker M and smaller Speaker S are both available in four color options, including orange and turquoise. Both speakers offer up to 18 hours of battery life, have an IP68 water and dust resistance rating, and can have their sound profile customized through the Nothing X app. That customizability extends to the design of the CMF Speaker Series, too. The multifunction knob on the front that controls volume and playback and the speaker’s entire front panel, including the vertical flap on top that can be used for hanging, can be easily removed and swapped with an alternate color or a completely different design. CMF plans to release the official design file so modders can 3D print their own unique customizations. [Image: Don’t like the color of the Speaker S or M? You can swap out the front plate and knobs. Don’t like the design? You can 3D print yourself a complete replacement. Other features include a dual-device connection for quickly jumping back and forth between two wireless audio sources Bluetooth 6, fast pairing using NFC, Google Fast Pair, or Microsoft Swift Pair, and audio over a USB-C cable. You can also pair two of the Speaker S or two of the Speaker M (you can’t mix and match) for a left-and-right stereo mode, or synchronize the full mix to several other speakers simultaneously, even from other companies, using an Auracast-based party mode.

articles.title: Microsoft’s new AI chip makes it less reliant on Nvidia’s GPUs
articles.summary: The new Maia 300 chip will start rolling out to production AI workloads in 2027.
articles.body: Microsoft is announcing its third-generation Maia in-house AI chip today, designed to be the “primary AI inference system” for Microsoft’s products and services. Maia 300 not only improves the cost and efficiency of running AI workloads in the cloud, it’s also more capable of handling the latest reasoning models and agentic tasks. Maia 300 will start being rolled out to production in 2027, and it has been designed with efficiency in mind. “We expect Maia 300 to deliver 40 percent more tokens per megawatt compared to leading GPU-based systems,” says Scott Guthrie, executive vice president of Microsoft’s cloud group. “And in a full 96-accelerator configuration, it delivers up to 7x the rack-scale token throughput of Maia 200.” These efficiency improvements will allow Microsoft to rely mainly on its in-house AI chips soon, instead of ones from Nvidia and AMD. “We will scale our Azure Maia family to multi-gigawatt deployments starting in 2027, making Maia the primary AI inference system for Microsoft products and services,” says Guthrie. [Image: Maia 300 chips will start being used for production workloads in 2027. Maia 300 is a successor to the 200, which was only announced in January. Maia 200 is already running on production AI workloads across Microsoft, including Microsoft Copilot, GitHub Copilot, Microsoft Foundry, and Microsoft’s own AI models. “Maia 200 is the best performing AI infrastructure in our fleet, measured in real world metrics for AI services,” says Guthrie. “Maia 300 is a complete AI system designed for the new types of AI workloads emerging today: Long-context reasoning, latency-sensitive conversational experiences, and sustained, multi-step agentic tasks.” Microsoft is using a new chiplet architecture to get its all-important efficiency gains. Built on TSMC’s N2P process node, the latest Maia 300 architecture separates compute, memory controller, and I/O functions. “This increases the silicon area dedicated to compute performance and allows each function to use the technology best suited to its role,” says the Azure hardware and infrastructure team. Maia 300 is also a key part of Microsoft’s own AI model work, and could help the company achieve its goal of catching up with Google DeepMind, OpenAI, and Anthropic. “We have to work across the full stack, all the way down to the silicon,” says Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman. “At that scale we need a platform that we own, and that we co-design with our models. That’s why running our Microsoft AI models on top of the Maia chip is a critical focus for our team.”

articles.title: The Fitbit Edge is for folks who don’t want to go totally screenless
articles.summary: The highly leaked $179.99 Fitbit Edge is now official. The middle-of-the-road tracker keeps the Air’s simple design but adds some of the Pixel Watch’s smarts.
articles.body: The Fitbit Edge may not be Google’s best-kept fitness-tracking secret, but as of today, its existence is official. The tracker sits smack-dab between the recently launched Fitbit Air and the more powerful Google Pixel Watch 5 in the company’s current wearable lineup. Basically, if you have smartwatch fatigue but don’t want to give up notifications, this is Google’s answer to the aging Fitbit Charge 6. Much of the Edge’s specs were previously leaked, but the tracker has a 46 percent larger OLED display compared to the Charge 6, a physical side button, and is a smidge thicker at 11.5mm. It also sports a replaceable battery that gets about a week on a single charge, though that estimate drops to two days if you enable the always-on display. The tracker uses the same proprietary charger as the Air, and can also get about a day’s worth of battery in five minutes. (A full charge takes 90 minutes.) For health tracking, the Edge has an EKG sensor for atrial fibrillation detection, a skin temperature sensor, SpO2 and optical heart rate sensors, plus your typical motion tracking sensors. As for dust and water resistance, the Edge is rated IP68 and is safe for swimming up to 5ATM. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: There are a few notable hardware omissions. The Edge doesn’t have a mic or speaker, so you can’t take calls from the wrist even though you can see who’s calling on the screen. Also, unlike the Charge 6, it lacks an NFC chip for contactless payments. The latter is a bit disappointing, given that the Edge essentially replaces the Charge 6 and is $20 more expensive at $179.99. That price does, however, include three months of Google Health Premium. The new Fitbit offers improved automatic workout tracking and GPS compared to the Charge 6. The former is a revised motion model that’ll also come to the Air. Beyond supporting racket sports, it pulls in location data and routines to make inferences about activities. For example, if you go to a tennis court, it’ll assume any activity logged there is tennis. If you regularly do yoga on Tuesday mornings, it’ll infer that’s what your activity is. Google says the new model means auto activity tracking is twice as accurate and supports over 100 activities. The Edge’s GPS tracking is also purportedly 40 percent more accurate — though it’s not using the same software-based post-processing update that Google introduced with the Pixel Watch 5. This increased accuracy mostly comes from on-device improvements to the Edge. It’ll also support turn-by-turn directions. [Image: [Image: The Edge and Fitbit Air are also getting metal link and mesh straps to give a more jewelry-like look. Feature-wise, the device is meant for people who want glanceable information, with some but not all the bells and whistles of a smartwatch. The Edge borrows much of the Pixel Watch’s design language as far as widgets and user interface go. It’s not running Wear OS, though; this is a redesigned Fitbit OS. It’ll also get the same Google Health software updates for features like blood pressure trends and insulin resistance levels. As far as non-fitness tracking features go, it has a clock, timers, alarms, media controls, and push notifications. It also supports heart rate broadcasting to certain gym equipment. Despite the screen, the overall look is more in line with the Air. The Edge will launch with several types of straps so you can adjust the style to fit various occasions, including metal links to give it more of a jewelry-like feel. (Speaking of jewelry-like styling, the Air is also getting a new metal mesh strap that costs $69.99 and is available October 27th.) As with the Air and Pixel Watch 5, there’ll be a Stephen Curry edition of the Edge that will cost $219.99.

articles.title: The OnePlus 16 is the company’s most interesting phone in years
articles.summary: But it’s not launching in the US or Europe.
articles.body: Today the OnePlus 16 launched in China, the company’s first flagship phone since quitting both the US and European markets this summer. As luck would have it, it also looks like the company’s best phone in some time. Like most OnePlus phones, the 16 is positioned around performance, with a Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 chipset, and up to 1TB of storage and 16GB of RAM. That’s backed up by an enormous 9,000mAh silicon-carbon battery, one of the biggest seen in any Android flagship yet. 100W wired and 50W wireless charging complete the power setup. On the display front, the phone jumps to a 185Hz OLED panel for the first time. That’ll not only be used for 185fps gaming in compatible titles, but can also run at up to 165Hz throughout the system UI — a first for high refresh rate panels like this. [Image: Even the cameras, not usually OnePlus’ strong suit, have had a meaningful upgrade. The main camera has a higher resolution (200 megapixels), larger sensor (1/1.4-inch-type), and faster aperture (f/1.4) than the OnePlus 15’s. That should help, given we found that phone’s camera had frustrating “imitations in low light.” 50-megapixel ultrawide and telephoto cameras round out the rear trio, and the latter also enjoys a big bump to a 1/1.95-inch sensor. [Image: There’s a design flourish too, with the phone’s silver finish including LED lighting that features a big “16” and what the company claims is a set of galactic coordinates. While the shapes of the lights are fixed, they’ll reportedly flash with different rhythms to notify you of calls, messages, battery level, and more. The OnePlus 16 is available in China starting from ¥5,699 (about $850). With OnePlus no longer in either the US or Europe, there’s no hope of a launch for the 16 in either market.

articles.title: Android is the best and worst thing about Googlebooks
articles.summary: As an Android phone reviewer and expert, I want to love Googlebooks — but they don’t make it easy.
articles.body: My first week with the new Android-powered laptops has been about as rocky as anyone’s, but I’ve slowly learned to like them, even if love still feels a ways off. Every moment that’s impressed me has been thanks to Android, whether I’ve been accessing a native version of a useful app or quickly checking my phone notifications from the laptop user interface. But man, sometimes it just sucks. Phone connectivity is flaky, app casting is awkward, and file-sharing seems to be flat-out broken. And that’s just the interaction between a Googlebook and a phone — I have a whole other set of gripes about the limitations of native Android apps on a $1,000 laptop. If Googlebooks ever become a success, Android is going to get the credit. But if it all goes wrong, that’s exactly where the blame will lie too. So far, success feels a lot further away than failure. Getting started [Image: During setup you can copy every app from your phone, or just a selection. The Googlebook setup process is Android through-and-through. It’s similarly quick, just a few minutes from beginning to end, including time to register biometric logins, log into a Google account, and connect it to a phone to find your apps and backups. There’s a little variation in the exact setup between the Asus and HP models I’ve been testing, but mostly just whether it defaults to installing every app from your phone or only the desktop-optimized ones. Things get janky once you’re into the OS, though. Even if you use an Android 17 phone to set up the laptop, it’s unlikely to remain connected afterwards for features like file sharing and app casting. Fully pairing either of my Googlebooks to a phone has required toggling cross-device settings on both devices, multiple restarts, and the occasional prayer, until the two devices find each other. Moving to a new Wi-Fi network broke things for me all over again, requiring a restart of the Googlebook to get the devices back talking to each other — and yes, they need to be on the same Wi-Fi network to talk, and to have Bluetooth enabled too, so the connection won’t work when you’re offline. My Asus Googlebook has now formed a pretty reliable connection to an Oppo phone I’ve been reviewing, though it still refuses to recognize any other phones; my HP model flits between that Oppo and the Vivo X Fold 6, occasionally connecting to both at once. Yesterday, for the first time all week, it connected to my Pixel 11 Pro Fold, after both laptops had stubbornly ignored that phone for days — even though it’s Google’s own hardware. Going native [Image: Downloadable episodes! On a laptop! This low key might be my favorite thing about Googlebooks. I’ve loved elements of the Googlebook experience. It’s great being able to access quick, compact, desktop versions of apps I’d normally be stuck using through a web browser on my MacBook. It’s even better that some of those apps have different functionality for being mobile versions: being able to download series from HBO Max or Netflix and watch them offline means a Googlebook could replace my Android tablet, which is mostly just a device for watching movies on planes at this point. But many, many more apps are a headache to use on an Android laptop. Some don’t have desktop-optimized versions — the mobile version of Slack is truly unworkable in a desktop environment, and Adobe’s Android apps are pale shadows of their desktop selves. Others claim to be “Optimized for desktop” in the Play Store, but in practice that usually means they’ve stretched the UI to fit a desktop scale and included basic mouse and keyboard support — “basic” being the operative word, with most not recognizing right-clicks or occasionally shifting into a portrait view. “Made for desktop” seems to be the only Play Store tag that really counts for much, and I’ve only seen it on a handful of apps. [Image: Some apps claim to be “Made for desktop,” everything else is likely to feel at least a little awkward. Even Google’s own apps are often limited. Chrome is the worst offender, since you’re likely to use it so much. Google insists this is a desktop version of the browser, but it lacks feature parity with other platforms: there’s no support for switching profiles, opening tabs in a split view, or creating custom search engine shortcuts. Those are just the omissions I’ve run into from my daily MacBook workflow, and there are no doubt countless more. And despite Google’s promise that Chromebooks offer the “entire Play Store library,” that isn’t entirely true. I’ve already run into two apps that I simply can’t install from the Play Store — Bluesky and the login authorization tool Okta. It’s not an Intel issue either, as Google alluded to on Monday: the Arm-based HP Googlebook also won’t run either app. My laptop needs aren’t complex: I spend 90 percent of my time on my work MacBook Air inside Chrome and Slack, and most of the rest in Photoshop or Lightroom. But all four are subpar on a Googlebook right now, and it’s all because they’re fundamentally Android apps that can’t compete with true desktop alternatives. Casting confusion If Android apps on your laptop aren’t enough, Googlebooks also let you cast the Android apps on your phone to your laptop. [Image: A dedicated app drawer shows everything installed on your connected phone. Some version of Android app casting or mirroring has been around before on both Windows and Chromebooks. The difference in Google’s implementation is that instead of mirroring the whole phone UI, you cast specific apps, either through a dedicated app drawer in the taskbar or by tapping into a synced notification from your phone. Those apps still run on the phone itself — which gets a notification that an app is casting — but are controlled via the PC. It’s not well-suited to streaming music or video, or running multiple apps at once, but that doesn’t seem to be the intent anyway. Where casting shines is in quickly dipping into an app without reaching for your phone and unlocking it, like updating a payment in the settlement app Splitwise or sending a quick message in WhatsApp. I’ve really enjoyed being able to dive in and out of a phone task from my laptop, while minimizing the risk of getting distracted by Instagram. Casting is clever and mostly works well, but I think I’ve found it useful because I’m new to the Googlebook and haven’t set every app up yet. Google argues it’s designed for apps you might want to use from your laptop but wouldn’t want to install there, but that’s a pretty short list, especially given that installing an Android app is generally quick, painless, and a minimal drain on storage. Long-term, I’m not sure how often I’d want to cast a mobile app when I could just install a native version, especially since you can’t copy and paste between native apps and cast versions, or access the Googlebook file system when casting. [Image: Casting Bluesky from the phone just doesn’t work, made worse because the Bluesky app is unavailable for Googlebooks otherwise. Even when the cross-device connection runs smoothly, some apps — especially secure ones like my authorization app or banking app — won’t run. Others try to open but don’t work: my credit card app breaks on bootup, while Bluesky renders text illegibly. Casting some apps even create rendering issues when I next open them back on the actual phone. The rest is a mess too Then there are the other problems. Continue On lets you start a task on your phone and pick it up on the Googlebook. It’s great when it works, but that’s rare. Only a handful of apps are supported, and even those trigger inconsistently. It works when I open a Google Drive document, but only sporadically in Gmail, and so far never for Calendar. Notifications are powerful, but messy, with phone and laptop notifications mixed together. Phone notifications open via app casting, but the system gets confused easily. For various reasons, right now my Slack notifications open a casted phone app rather than the native Googlebook app; WhatsApp notifications don’t come through even from my phone; and I can either get notifications for my work Gmail account or my personal one, but not both at once. File transfer is entirely broken. While I can see my phone’s storage as a drive inside the file manager, accessing those files is near-impossible. It can take minutes to load up the file system, and minutes more to open or transfer a single 5MB photo. It’s completely unusable. This should be fixable, at least. Quick Share — Android’s equivalent to AirDrop — is also supported, and the same files that take minutes over file transfer share in seconds with Quick Share. [Image: [Image: It’s the Googlebook in a nutshell: the idea is wonderful, the execution entirely lacking. A week in, I’m learning to work around the kinks and headaches of this odd little OS, finding ways to make the most of it and to maximize those moments when my laptop and my phone just work together. When it clicks, it feels like the payoff to a decade and a half of using Android every day. Right now, that feeling doesn’t hit nearly as often as it needs to, and certainly not enough to make up for the countless times Android just feels broken in this form factor. The question is whether Google — a company with a deserved reputation for giving up when the going gets tough — has the commitment to see this through and turn things around. It’ll need its own teams to fix what’s broken, third-party developers to pledge support en masse, and a rethink of how to integrate native apps with casting from a phone. When I first saw the Googlebooks a few weeks ago, I really thought one might be my next laptop. After spending a week with them, I’m not so sure. I certainly wouldn’t buy a Googlebook as they are right now, but I wouldn’t rule out an Android laptop in the future — the execution just needs to catch up to the idea. articles.title: Fitbit Edge is Google’s middle ground between Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Google’s newest wearable costs $179.99 and has a sleek feel like the Fitbit Air but with an OLED display.
articles.body:
Google’s Fitbit lineup expanded on Monday with the introduction of the Fitbit Edge, a new wearable that’s positioned between the Fitbit Air and Pixel Watch.

Priced at $179.99, it combines the Fitbit Air’s slim band with an OLED display for checking map directions, notifications, weather, and music controls.

Like the Pixel Watch and Fitbit Air, the Edge works with Google Health Coach, powered by Gemini. (You’ll need a Google Health Premium subscription to use it.) The coach can use your fitness, health, and medical information to put together weekly routines and workout plans, then adjust them around your schedule.

It also comes with Google’s Health Guardian feature, which is designed to spot notable changes in health measurements over time, including indicators related to blood pressure and insulin resistance. (The company announced these features at the Pixel Watch 5 launch in August.)

Google says the Fitbit Edge can automatically recognize and log up to 100 activities, including runs, bike rides and walks. The company explains it uses context from your movement to work out what you’re doing and add it to your weekly goals. Plus, the device supports more than 50 exercise modes and can offer on-screen prompts during workouts, such as a nudge to push harder or take a breather.

The Fitbit Edge’s built-in GPS is 40% more accurate than the previous generation, the company claims, which should make it easier to track outdoor runs. Google says sleep-stage detection is also 15% more accurate than on earlier generations, helping the device provide better sleep summaries and coaching tips.

Meanwhile, the battery is rated for up to seven days on a charge, and the wearable is water-resistant to 50 meters.

The Fitbit Edge is available to preorder through the Google Store, with store availability set for October 27.

Color choices include Obsidian, Fog, Olive, and Canyon. There’s also a Stephen Curry Special Edition, priced at $219.99.

articles.title: Shane Gillis joked about women's gym clothes on 'SNL.' Dan Levy isn't laughing.
articles.summary: The "Schitt's Creek" star said jokes that objectify women contribute to a culture that minimizes sexual assault.
articles.body:
Dan Levy has called for more men to stand up for women after being left "speechless" by Shane Gillis's Saturday Night Live monologue, in which the comedian joked that women "dress like whores" at the gym.

Gillis, who hosted SNL alongside musical guest Rosalía on Oct. 10, said , "I haven't been to the gym in so long. I didn't know women just dress like whores now?" He went on to describe women's gym shorts before joking that men were "not allowed to look."

The comments sparked widespread backlash with Levy, the costar and co-creator of Schitt's Creek , condemning the remarks as misogynistic, saying that the objectification of women contributes to a culture in which sexual assault is not taken seriously.

In a video posted to Instagram , he said, "Women wearing short shorts to the gym does not make them whores. It makes the men calling them 'whores' misogynists. There's a difference there.

"By the way, I've seen more men's nipples at the gym than I've ever seen women showing their bodies off, but I'm speechless that something like that can exist on live national television.

"And to be perfectly honest, more men need to be standing up in opposition to it because it's complacency that has created the environment in which women are sexually assaulted, and it's a 'conversation' as opposed to a crime.

"Men need to be defending women more. This is not a women's issue. This is an everybody issue. Because the more that men objectify women in the media, the more that other men see them as objects and treat them as objects. They are superior human beings to men, OK? And I'm sorry if this gets me in trouble with the internet, but f***."

Female celebrities voiced support for Levy in the comments, including Sarah Michelle Gellar , Alyssa Milano , Elizabeth Banks and Hacks actor Hannah Einbinder .

Model Tess Holliday thanked Levy for "speaking up," writing , "The way men and other women hating folks view our bodies is absolutely destroying our society. We are taught from an early age to not dress a certain way or look a certain way, to not entice them or provoke them. No where is safe not even in our own bodies, not in gyms, our homes, minding our own business. Where does it end?"

According to Entertainment Weekly , former SNL cast member Victoria Jackson defended the controversial joke, saying, "He's right about gym girls dressing like 'whores.' When did 'camel toe' become acceptable gym fashion and grocery shopping attire?"

Saturday marked Gillis's third time hosting SNL , a show with which he has a controversial history. In 2019, he was hired as a cast member but was fired before making his debut after podcast clips resurfaced in which he used racist slurs and made homophobic remarks.

After the clips resurfaced, Gillis described himself as a "comedian who pushes boundaries" and said he was willing to apologize to "anyone who's actually offended" by his comedy.

"If you go through my 10 years of comedy, most of it bad, you're going to find a lot of bad misses," he said at the time. "I'm happy to apologize to anyone who's actually offended by anything I've said. My intention is never to hurt anyone but I am trying to be the best comedian I can be and sometimes that requires risks."

Gillis's latest stint on the show drew unflattering reviews from critics. Variety 's Marlow Stern described his monologue as "meandering," adding, "Gillis has shown considerable comedy chops in his stand-up specials and hosting the ESPYs, but nailing an SNL monologue seems to be elusive for him."

The Guardian described it as "a watered-down version of his normal material, with just enough bro-y but self-aware edginess thrown in to appease his fans and uphold his image as an anti-woke icon."

The A.V. Club said Gillis "muddled through another sub-par hosting performance," while the New York Times said the comedian dropping an F-bomb during a sketch "might end up being the most memorable moment" from the episode.
